translation: "Shut up," the optician said louder and quickened his pace, "Selma finds very few things threatening or unsightly.
He was absolutely right about this, but unfortunately he had said more than he should have replied to the voices.
But they might find love, of all things, unsightly, the voices hissed--there's a reason why the truth was kept hidden so long.
"Cowardice is what it is," said the optician and switched his leather bag to the other hip because both the jostling of bag and voices were starting to hurt him.
"Prudence is what it is," replied them, "Fear can sometimes be a good adviser", they suggested while humming theme tunes from early evening TV shows.
The optician now began slowing down.
The journey to Selma's house which usually would take ten minutes suddenly felt like a day's trip with an awful lot of luggage.
That was true.
The dog was the color of slushy snow, it was faded gray and shaggy like a purebred Irish Wolfhound with nothing else mixed in.
Its body was still small, but its paws were as large as bear paws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma still stood by the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as if he were a gift shop.
Farmer Häubel was firmly convinced that Death would be polite, just as Farmer Häubel himself had been all his life.
He was certain that Death would not snatch away his life but gently take it from his hands.
He imagined Death knocking softly, only opening the door a crack and asking "May I?", to which Farmer Häubel would of course affirm.
"Certainly," Farmer Häubel would say, "do come in", and then death would enter.
He'd stand by the bed of Farmer Häubel and ask: "Does this moment work for you? Otherwise, I can come by at a later time".

Farmer Haübel would sit up and say, "No no, right now is quite perfect for me", "let's not postpone it again—who knows when you might make it back", and death would then seat himself on the chair placed ready at the end of the bed.
In anticipation he'd apologize forthe coolness of his hands which as farmer Haübel knew wouldn't bother him at all; then he would rest one hand on farmer Haübel's closed eyes.
The people in the village were unsettled, it was apparent even though most of them tried not to show it.
This morning, a few hours after Selma's dream, the villagers moved as if there were black ice on all paths, not only outside but also inside their homes—in their kitchens and living rooms.
They acted as though their own bodies had become utterly foreign to them, as if all their joints had become inflamed and every object they handled was highly combustible.
All day long they viewed their lives with suspicion and scrutinized that of others where possible.

They continually looked behind themselves to check whether someone might be lurking there with murderous intent—someone who had lost his mind and therefore had nothing significant left to lose—and then quickly returned their gaze forwards because such a person could also attack from the front.
They looked up above to rule out falling roof tiles, branches or heavy lamp shades.
They avoided all animals because they believed madness could break out more swiftly from them than from humans.

They stayed clear of even the gentlest cows—gods-forbid they might start kicking today; they gave wide berth to dogs—even those so elderly they could barely stand—out of fear that even these creatures might go after them at any moment with malicious intent today;
everything is possible on such days—you wouldn't put it past an aged dachshund tearing your throat out either;
this is no more absurd than rampant okapis running about after all.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, the villagers were mostly not superstitious.
They would casually do all that one shouldn't do in superstition:
They sat calmly under wall clocks, even though in superstition it can lead to death.
They slept with their heads toward the door, though that means in superstition you'll be carried out feet first through that very door soon.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year's Day, which Elsbeth warned was akin to suicide or aiding and abetting murder, according to superstition.
They were not startled when an owl hooted at night when a horse strongly sweated in its stable or when a dog howled at night with its head down.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes without any stops.

Since our first train journey, we always played the same game: We stood with our backs to the windows by the opposite train doors, Martin shut his eyes, while I looked out of the window of the train door behind Martin.
In first grade, I listed everything I saw during our journey for Martin to try and memorize them all.

It went very well so that in second grade I stopped listing things and Martin was able to recite almost everything that I could see through the foggy window despite him facing away from it: "Wire factory," he'd say just as we passed by it.

"What else could it have been?"
Selma said, mentioning that an okapi is hardly to be mistaken for another animal.
"Actually," I argued, "it might have also been a misshapen cow, a wrongly assembled giraffe, a freak of nature.
The stripes and the reddish color you can't recognize these very clearly at night when everything is rather blurry.
"That's nonsense," Selma said while rubbing her forehead, "That's unfortunately nonsense, Luise.
She put a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it and put it in my lunch box.
"Do you remember exactly when you dreamt this?"
I asked.
"Around three o'clock," said Selma.

She had jolted awake after the image of the okapi retreated sitting upright in bed she found herself staring at her nightdress which in her dream she had been wearing on Uhlheck and then at the clock: three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take this too seriously", Selma stated although she sounded like a TV detective dismissing an anonymous note as unimportant.
"What's the matter?"
I asked.
"Nothing," Selma trilled, opening the refrigerator and pulling out a pack of sliced cheese and a liverwurst, waving them in the air.
"What would you like on your sandwich for school today?" she trilled.
"Little mouse," she added in an unnervingly cheerful voice.
"Cheese, please," I said, "What's wrong with you?"
"Nothing," Selma repeated cheerily, "Just like I said".
She spread some butter on a slice of bread while still bustling around; as a result, her wrist knocked over the cheese from our sideboard down onto the floor.
Suddenly still, Selma looked down at the package of cheese as if it was something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and each time someone had died afterwards, so we were convinced that the dream of an okapi and death were invariably linked.
That's how our minds work.
It can quickly establish a solid link between the most unrelated things.
Coffee pots and shoelaces, for example, or deposit bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me bedtime stories with happy endings.
When I was younger, I used to grip her wrist after hearing the stories, placing my thumb on her pulse and imagining that the entire world was moving to the rhythm of Selma's heartbeat.

I pictured the optician grinding lenses, Martin lifting a weight, Elsbeth cutting her hedge; the shopkeeper arranging juice cartons; my mother stacking up pine branches; my father stamping prescriptions everyone doing these things exactly to the rhythm of Selma's heart.
This always reliably put me to sleep.
But now that I am ten years old, Selma thought it was time for me to outgrow this habit.
